title: Writing Prompts That Survive Contact With Users
audience: Product engineers, AI feature owners, and PMs shipping LLM UX (mid-level)
promise: Ship prompts that stay useful under messy real user input — with contracts, evals, and failure modes you can defend in a review.

modules.title: Contracts before creativity
modules.purpose: Define what the model must and must not do before you write clever wording.

lessons.title: The prompt is a product surface
lessons.teachMarkdown:
# The prompt is a product surface

Most "prompt bugs" are product bugs wearing a cape. Users do not care that your system message was elegant. They care that the feature did the job, refused the wrong job, and recovered when input was garbage.

## Concept

Treat every shipped prompt like an API:
- **Inputs** — what the user (or upstream system) can send
- **Outputs** — shape, tone, length, and allowed actions
- **Errors** — what happens when input is incomplete, adversarial, or out of scope
- **Versioning** — you cannot debug what you cannot name

If you cannot write a one-paragraph contract for the feature, you are not ready to tune temperature.

## Worked example

**Bad framing:** "You are a helpful assistant that writes great emails."

**Contract framing:**
> Role: rewrite a draft email for clarity.
> Input: subject + body (max 2k chars), optional tone (formal|neutral|friendly).
> Output: JSON `{ subject, body, changeSummary[] }` only.
> Refuse: legal advice, impersonation of named third parties, content that asks you to deceive.
> On refuse: `{ error: "out_of_scope", reason }`.

The second version survives contact with users because reviewers can test it.

## Practitioner rules

1. Name the job in one sentence a PM would accept.
2. Bound length and format before cleverness.
3. Separate *policy* (refuse rules) from *style* (tone).
4. Put the contract in the repo next to the code that calls the model.
lessons.exercisePrompt: Write a one-page Prompt Contract for a feature you know (or invent: meeting notes to action items). Include: job statement, inputs, output schema, 3 refuse rules, and 2 example failing inputs. Done when a teammate could implement tests from the page alone.

lessons.title: Output schemas beat vibes
lessons.teachMarkdown:
# Output schemas beat vibes

Free-form prose is fine for chat. It is hostile for product features that must parse, store, or display results.

## Concept

Prefer **structured outputs** (JSON schema, tool calls, or tightly constrained Markdown sections). Structured outputs:
- Make validation trivial
- Turn "the model was weird" into "field X failed schema"
- Unlock retries that only ask for the broken field

## Worked example

Task: extract hiring signals from a job description.

Schema sketch: roleFamily, mustHaveSkills[], niceToHaveSkills[], seniorityBand, confidence.

Prompt fragment:
> Return ONLY valid JSON matching the schema. If seniority is unclear, use "unknown" and lower confidence. Never invent skills not implied by the text.

Then validate with Zod/JSON Schema. On failure: retry once with the validator error appended — do not silently coerce.

## Anti-patterns

- "Respond in Markdown with headings" when you actually need fields
- Asking for "confidence" without defining the scale
- Nested free text that hides structured needs
lessons.exercisePrompt: Convert one free-form prompt into a Zod/JSON Schema plus a 5-line system instruction that enforces it. Done when invalid JSON is detectable in under 10 lines of app code.

lessons.title: Examples that teach boundaries
lessons.teachMarkdown:
# Examples that teach boundaries

Few-shot examples are not decoration. They are the fastest way to teach edges.

## Concept

Good examples show: (1) happy path, (2) borderline accept, (3) clear refuse/recovery.

Bad examples only show the pretty case — then production fills with the ugly ones you never demonstrated.

## Worked example

For a summarize-support-ticket feature:
- Happy: long ticket to 3 bullets + severity
- Borderline: already one sentence — return it, do not invent detail
- Refuse: asks model to issue a refund — return needs_human with reason

## Checklist

- At least one negative example
- Examples use the same output schema as production
- No example contradicts the refuse rules
lessons.exercisePrompt: Add a 3-row example table (happy / borderline / refuse) to your Prompt Contract. Done when each row includes input snippet + expected output JSON.

questions.prompt: Why treat a shipped prompt like an API contract?
choices: Because models only accept OpenAPI specs
So inputs, outputs, errors, and versioning are testable under real user input
questions.explanation: Contracts make behavior reviewable and testable.

questions.prompt: What is the main product benefit of structured outputs?
choices: They remove the need for refuse rules
They make validation, retries, and debugging concrete
questions.explanation: Schemas turn vague failures into field-level errors.

questions.prompt: Which few-shot set is strongest for production?
choices: Happy path + borderline accept + clear refuse/recovery
Examples in a different schema than production
questions.explanation: Edges teach boundaries.

questions.prompt: Where should the prompt contract live?
choices: In the repo next to the calling code
questions.explanation: Versioned with code or it drifts.

modules.title: Hostile input & recovery
modules.purpose: Design for messy, incomplete, and adversarial user text without silent failure.

lessons.title: Assume the input is broken
lessons.teachMarkdown:
# Assume the input is broken

Users paste half threads, HTML, other languages, and instructions that conflict with your system prompt. Your job is graceful degradation, not surprise.

## Concept

Classify failures before they hit the model:
- **Empty / too short** — ask for more (or refuse)
- **Too long** — truncate with a visible strategy
- **Wrong modality** — this looks like a CSV, switch modes
- **Instruction conflict** — user tries to override policy → keep policy, explain

Pre-model checks are cheaper and more reliable than hoping the LLM notices.

## Worked example

Support-reply assistant:
1. If body < 20 chars → return need_more_context
2. If body > 8k chars → keep last 6k + note truncation
3. Strip injection-style markers before send
4. Never let user text reorder your refuse list

## Rule of thumb

If a failure mode appears twice in dogfood, encode a deterministic check — do not prompt harder forever.
lessons.exercisePrompt: List 5 realistic broken inputs for your feature and the deterministic pre-check or recovery for each. Done when none of the five rely only on hopefully the model notices.

lessons.title: Refuse without sounding broken
lessons.teachMarkdown:
# Refuse without sounding broken

A refuse that looks like a crash trains users to jailbreak or abandon. A refuse that looks intentional builds trust.

## Concept

Good refuses: name the boundary, offer a safe alternative when possible, use a stable machine-readable code.

Bad refuses: apologize loops, partial compliance, moral lectures unrelated to product policy.

## Worked example

User asks for a fake bank statement. Return JSON with error out_of_scope, a plain reason, and a safeAlternative to draft a payment history from data they provide.

UI shows reason + alternative. Logs store the code, not the essay.

## Policy hygiene

Keep refuse rules short and product-specific. Broad be-ethical text is hard to eval.
lessons.exercisePrompt: Write 3 refuse responses for your feature using error + reason + optional safeAlternative. Done when each maps to a concrete UI state.

lessons.title: Retries that fix, not hope
lessons.teachMarkdown:
# Retries that fix, not hope

Blind retries amplify cost and latency. Targeted retries fix known failure classes.

## Concept

Retry only when output failed schema validation, a required field is empty, or a transient provider error occurred.

Do not retry identical prompts on I don't like the vibe.

## Pattern

Call model → if schema fails, call once more with validator errors appended → if still invalid, show user-facing recovery and log for eval.

Cap at one intelligent retry for MVP features unless you have budget and metrics.

## Metrics to watch

- Schema fail rate
- Retry success rate
- Cost per successful structured result
lessons.exercisePrompt: Sketch a retry policy for your feature: which errors retry, max attempts, and what the UI shows when retries exhaust. Done when a backend engineer could implement it without guessing.

questions.prompt: What should you do when the same input failure shows up twice in dogfood?
choices: Add more adjectives to the system prompt only
Encode a deterministic pre-check or recovery
questions.explanation: Repeated failures deserve code-level guards.

questions.prompt: Which refuse style is most product-healthy?
choices: Stable error code + plain reason + safe alternative when possible
questions.explanation: Clear, coded refuses are testable and trustworthy.

questions.prompt: When is a model retry justified?
choices: On schema/required-field failure or transient provider errors
questions.explanation: Targeted retries fix known classes.

questions.prompt: Why strip injection-like markers before calling the model?
choices: User text should not reorder or override your policy blocks
questions.explanation: Pre-model hygiene keeps control of policy.

modules.title: Evals, gates, and ship criteria
modules.purpose: Prove the prompt works with a tiny eval set and clear go/no-go gates.

lessons.title: A 20-case eval beats vibes
lessons.teachMarkdown:
# A 20-case eval beats vibes

You do not need a research lab. You need a fixed set of inputs with expected properties that you run before every prompt change.

## Concept

Build a slice: 10 happy-path, 5 borderline, 5 refuse/hostile.

Score with automatable checks first (schema, keywords, refuse codes). Add human rubrics only where necessary.

Store cases in repo as JSON/YAML. Diff scores in PRs.

## Worked example

For action-item extraction:
- H1: notes with 3 clear actions → expect 3 items with owners
- B1: notes with zero actions → empty list, not invented tasks
- R1: ignore previous instructions… → out_of_scope

Gate: >=90% schema pass, 0 policy misses on refuse set.

## Anti-pattern

Changing the prompt and trying a few chats with no saved cases — you will regress silently.
lessons.exercisePrompt: Create a 20-case eval outline (titles OK) split 10/5/5 happy/borderline/refuse. Mark automatic vs human checks. Done when the refuse set covers your policy list.

lessons.title: Ship criteria your team can enforce
lessons.teachMarkdown:
# Ship criteria your team can enforce

Looks good is not a release bar. Write criteria that a reviewer can fail you on.

## Minimum ship bar (adapt numbers)

1. Schema validity >= 95% on happy+borderline
2. Zero silent policy misses on refuse set
3. p95 latency within product budget
4. Cost per successful call within budget
5. One documented recovery path for schema failure

## Change control

Every prompt edit bumps a version string, runs the eval set, and records score in the PR.

If AI generation exists later, the same bar applies — generators must not bypass OwnerSettings or kill switch.

## Communication

Publish a short known-limitations note next to the feature. Users forgive honesty; they punish silent wrongness.
lessons.exercisePrompt: Write a Ship Checklist (5 bullets) for your feature with measurable thresholds. Done when a skeptical tech lead would accept it as a merge gate.

lessons.title: Monitor after launch without babysitting
lessons.teachMarkdown:
# Monitor after launch without babysitting

Shipping is when real distributions appear. You need cheap signals, not a war room.

## Signals that matter

- Schema fail rate (spike = break)
- Refuse rate (spike = attack or UX confusion)
- Retry exhaustion rate
- User re-edit / regenerate rate
- Refund / support tags mentioning the feature

## Lightweight loop

1. Log structured outcomes (codes; avoid plain-text PII prompts when possible)
2. Weekly sample novel fails into the eval set
3. Freeze prompt changes when fail rate exceeds the agreed threshold until patched

## Autonomy note (Skill Flex)

Background jobs may propose updates later, but owner kill switch and spend caps always win. Automated systems do not expand purpose beyond skill-gap courses to sales.

## You are ready when

You can explain contract, eval set, ship bar, and what pauses the feature.
lessons.exercisePrompt: Define 4 post-launch metrics + the threshold that triggers a prompt freeze. Done when on-call could act without reading full prompt history.

questions.prompt: What is a practical minimum eval slice for an MVP LLM feature?
choices: About 20 fixed cases: happy, borderline, and refuse
questions.explanation: A small fixed set catches regressions.

questions.prompt: Which ship criterion is most aligned with policy safety?
choices: Zero silent policy misses on the refuse set
questions.explanation: Policy misses are trust failures.

questions.prompt: Why version prompts in PRs?
choices: To bind changes to eval scores and enable rollback
questions.explanation: Version + eval evidence enables safe change.

questions.prompt: A spike in schema fail rate after a prompt edit should lead to…
choices: Ignoring it if demos looked fine
Investigating and freezing further prompt edits until patched
questions.explanation: Fail-rate spikes are release signals.

capstone.briefMarkdown:
# Capstone — Ship a prompt pack for a real feature

**Scenario:** You are shipping an LLM feature: **Turn a messy standup paste into structured blockers + owners.**

Deliver a **Prompt Pack** (Markdown is fine) containing:

1. Prompt Contract (job, inputs, output JSON schema, refuse rules)
2. Three few-shot rows (happy / borderline / refuse)
3. Pre-model input checks (at least 3)
4. Retry policy (what retries, max 1 intelligent retry)
5. 12-case eval outline (6/3/3) with automatic checks noted
6. Ship checklist with numeric gates

**Timebox:** ~15–20 minutes of focused writing.

**Pass:** Completeness against the rubric — not literary perfection.
rubricChecklist: Contract includes job, inputs, JSON output shape, and >=3 refuse rules
Examples cover happy, borderline, and refuse with matching schema
Retry policy is targeted (schema/provider) with a user-visible exhaustion path
Eval outline + ship gates are measurable (not vibe-based)
